content: A Nabothian cyst is a mucus-filled cyst that forms on the surface of the cervix. These cysts typically develop when new tissue growth obstructs the Nabothian glands of the cervix, leading to the entrapment of mucosal secretions in small subdermal pockets, which are usually 2–10 mm in diameter. Nabothian cysts are also referred to as Nabothian follicles, mucinous retention cysts, or epithelial inclusion cysts. They are named after Martin Naboth, a German anatomist (1675–1721), who described them in a 1707 treatise titled De sterilitate mulierum. However, they were first documented earlier by Guillaume Desnoues, a French surgeon (1650–1735). Clinically, Nabothian cysts often present as firm bumps on the surface of the cervix. Women may notice these cysts during the insertion of a diaphragm or cervical cap, or while performing a cervical self-check as part of fertility awareness practices. Gynecologists frequently identify these cysts during routine pelvic examinations. Nabothian cysts are generally considered harmless and often resolve spontaneously. Some women observe that the cysts appear and disappear in correlation with their menstrual cycle. If a woman is uncertain whether an anomaly on her cervix is a Nabothian cyst, it is advisable to consult a physician to rule out other potential conditions. In atypical cases, multiple large Nabothian cysts may be identified, and imaging techniques such as CT or MRI may be utilized for further evaluation. Treatment for Nabothian cysts is typically unnecessary unless the cysts grow significantly large and cause secondary symptoms. In such cases, a gynecologist may perform a colposcopy or biopsy to exclude malignancy or other underlying issues. If removal is deemed necessary, two common methods include electrocautery and cryotherapy. Complications associated with Nabothian cysts are rare. However, in some cases, they may be linked to chronic cervicitis, which is an inflammatory infection of the cervix.
